title: Yasa's night
hook: a rich young man wakes after a party, sickened, and walks out into the night (Vinaya, Mahavagga 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, not-self: five heaps, and none of them a fixed owner. Your line was not mine. Which feeling did you ask, is this me? Day sixty-five.

It's three in the morning. The party's over but nobody went home. There are people asleep on the couch, on the floor, someone snoring with a hand still around a cup. The music stopped a while ago. And you're the only one awake, looking at it all, and something turns in your stomach that isn't the food. Maybe you know that feeling. A young man named Yasa knew it. He was the son of a very rich family in Benares, with a house for every season and musicians who played for him through the night. One night he woke up before everyone else. And what he did next is today's story.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `THE ONLY ONE AWAKE.` → `A RICH YOUNG MAN NAMED YASA.`

segments.voice: The old monastic rulebook, the Vinaya, tells it vividly. Yasa wakes, and the lamps are still burning, and he sees the musicians and attendants asleep around him, sprawled in every direction, mouths open, instruments dropped. The text says it looked to him like a cemetery. And he cries out: how distressing this is, how oppressive. He puts on his golden slippers and walks out of the house, out of the city gate, into the dark. His feet take him toward the Deer Park. And the Buddha, the story says, is walking up and down in the open air before dawn. He hears Yasa's cry, and answers: this is not distressing, this is not oppressive. Come, Yasa, sit down. I'll teach you. So a young man in party clothes and golden slippers sits down on the ground with a wandering teacher, and listens, and something in him settles. Now, why does this story matter? Notice how much it sounds like another one. A young man of a rich family. Pleasure all around him. A night when he looks at sleeping bodies and sees the truth under the glitter. A walk out into the dark. That's the Buddha's own story, his great going forth. Yasa lives it in one night, and this time there's someone waiting on the road. And look at his name. Yasa means fame, or glory. The man named Fame found the party empty. The story doesn't stop at one person, either. His father comes searching, following the tracks of those golden slippers, and becomes the first lay follower to take the three refuges. His mother and his former wife become the first women lay followers. And Yasa's friends come looking for him too. Tomorrow, where that leads.
screen: `IT LOOKED LIKE A CEMETERY.` · `COME, YASA, SIT DOWN.` · `THE BUDDHA'S STORY IN ONE NIGHT.` · `HIS FAMILY FOLLOWS THE SLIPPERS.` · then, large: `WALK OUT OF THE PARTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing that has lost its shine. Settle and breathe. Think of something you keep doing that doesn't give you what it used to. An app you open without meaning to. A habit that's gone flat. A place you keep going because you always have. Picture it the way Yasa saw that room, with the lamps still on. You don't have to hate it. Just see it clearly, and imagine standing up and walking out the door. The bell holds the time.
Yasa's night. A rich young man wakes after a party, sees it clearly, walks out into the dark, and finds the Buddha on the road.
Your line: walk out of the party. Today, leave one thing early that has lost its shine, a scroll, a conversation, a habit, and see where your feet go. Day sixty-five.

howItsDone: Buddhists tell Yasa's story as one of the first conversions after the Deer Park, and remember his father as the first lay follower to take refuge in the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, as lay Buddhists still do today.

fork.setup: you're Yasa. it's before dawn, the party is over, and the room suddenly looks like a cemetery. what do you do?
options: wake everyone up and start again.
put on your slippers and walk out into the night.
fork.reveal: he walks out of the house and out of the city gate, toward the Deer Park, and finds the Buddha walking there before dawn.

original.note: Pali: fame, glory, renown. Sanskrit yaśas.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rich kid with a hangover.
what it means: a young man who sees through a life of pleasure in one night, walks out, and finds a teacher waiting.
what a scholar hears: Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.7–1.10: Yasa's night echoes the Buddha's own going forth; his father becomes the first lay follower to go for the three refuges.

notes: Retold in paraphrase from Mahavagga 1.7–1.10: three palaces, the cemetery image, the cry 'how distressing, how oppressive', the golden slippers, the Buddha walking in the open air, 'come, Yasa, sit down'. Confirm details and section numbers.
The Vinaya also says the Buddha made Yasa invisible to his father while the father was taught; omitted for length. Confirm the omission is acceptable.
Yasa's father as the first lay follower to take the three refuges (the two merchants on day 58 took two refuges, before the sangha existed). Confirm this distinction is right.
Yasa's name glossed as 'fame, glory' (Pali yasa, Sanskrit yaśas); confirm.
